thread.title: The End Of The Age Of Apple?

author: John M. Mason
title: The End Of The Age Of Apple?
text:
No sooner did I get my post out titled “ Big Tech: It’s Barely Getting Started ,” when I was faced with the question in an op-ed piece in the New York Times, “ Is This the End of the Age of Apple? ”
What happened in between?
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) announced a revenue shortfall and a downward revision in its forward guidance.
Apple’s stock price tanked and articles started appearing declaring the end of the world.
Or. at least the articles claimed that the future would not be so rosy.
The first headlines that came out cited Apple CEO Tim Cook’s alluding to the decline in performance due to President Trump’s tariff battles with the Chinese and the slowing growth of the Chinese economy.
But, later responses carried also added claims like these.
From the Financial Times : “A sudden dip in sales in China may be the biggest factor behind Apple’s drastic revenue shortfall, but the deeper issues the warning has raised about the iPhone will turn out to have a more lasting impact on the company.”
And in the Wall Street Journal : “Apple Inc. chief Tim Cook blamed China’s accelerating economic slowdown for stumbling iPhone sales that hurt its global revenue in the past quarter. The company’s problems run deeper in China and extend to markets beyond.”
The concern is captured in two aspects of the current situation. First, very little new or different has been done to the iPhone recently and with this innovation lag, consumers are lagging in interest and postponing the purchase of any new iPhone product.
Secondly, Apple’s pricing policies that used higher prices to make up for a lag in the sales of iPhones has taken Apple’s prices to very high levels in the market place.
This strategy has allowed Chinese rivals to challenge Apple’s position n the market place. For example, in the Wall Street Journal article cited above we read “Chinese rivals including Huawei Technologies Co. are selling feature-competitive smartphones at lower prices squeezing Apple’s share of the world’s largest smartphone market.”
The key idea, however, is that Apple is now lagging in innovation.
This is made clear in the New York Times piece cited above. The author, Kara Swisher, editor at large for the technology news website Recode, claims that “We need the next wave of innovation and we need it now.”
“Apple has hung the moon for investors for so long now that the idea of the company struggling sent the entire global stock market into a paroxysm of fear and plunging indexes.”
“Apple is not only a bellwether company in tech but also the most expertly managed one under Tim Cook.”
And, the frenzy increases, as Ms. Swisher quotes In Fried of Axios: “The problems Apple saw in China go far beyond just Apple, But Apple’s iPhone problems extend far beyond China, too.”
“Indeed.” Ms. Swisher adds, “The last big innovation explosion—the proliferation of the smartphone—is clearly ending.”
Where is the next big thing? Or, as Ms. Swisher concludes, “Where is that next spark that will light us all up?
So the market tanks, at least for one day.
But, there will be a next day, and another, and another.
There will be another “spark” that lights us all up.
This is what my post , cited above, was all about. Big Tech is just getting started.
I cited an expert that studies the area of innovation and he stated, “For all intents and purposes, we’re only 35 years into a 75- or 80-year process of moving from analog to digital.”
We are still closer to the beginning of the digital age than we are to it’s winding down. And, the growth and spread of information is pervasive. Information, over time, can creep into almost any space.
As I wrote this post, “what areas will ‘Big Tech’ be getting into?”
“Everything.”
Furthermore, “Big Tech is planning for a future far beyond any present-day turmoil.”
“There is so much that remains disrupted.”
In other words, to use the terminology of the economist, there are many, many missing markets out there and the hunt is on to find them, and serve them in whatever way possible.
What form will these innovations take?
Who knows. History has shown us that if we are less than halfway through a transitional age, like the age we are gong through, much is more to come and the “waves of innovation” may not be as startling or disrupting as the previous ones have. Or, then again, we may experience another major way or two. Think of artificial intelligence.
Before we get down on Apple and talk about the end of the age of Apple, or, before we begin to dismiss “Big Tech” we need to remember all that we are talking about and massive change the world is going through.
Yes, we do not know where the next major innovation is coming from, or what the next major innovation will be. We must find good leaders, leaders that are focused not only on what the next major innovation might be, but is also focused on the longer-run in terms of providing the openness and transparency needed in this modern, fast moving age.
I don’t believe that this is the end of the age of Apple, or, the end of the age of “Big Tech.” If ”Big Tech” is going to be getting into “everything,” Some of the further changes may be “major” ones, but, in reality, many, many more of the changes may just be small ones.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions.
